issues.legal_issue: Rule 10 of Order VIII of the Code of Civil Procedure is permissive and does not require a court to enter judgment merely because a defendant has failed to file a written statement.

Where one of several defendants has filed a written statement raising disputed issues, a court should ordinarily avoid decreeing the suit against another defendant under Rule 10 of Order VIII without resolving the controversy, absent extraordinary circumstances.

A decree may be challenged as inexecutable under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure only when it is a nullity for an inherent lack of jurisdiction patent on the face of the record, not merely because it is erroneous or procedurally irregular.

A court that decides a claim on its merits without first determining its competence to entertain the suit may act without inherent jurisdiction, rendering its order and resulting decree null and inexecutable.

A judgment under Rule 10 of Order VIII must state the reasoning required by section 2(9) and Order XX Rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, and a decree must follow a valid judgment that formally determines rights in controversy.

When a suit's maintainability is challenged, a court considering interim relief must record at least a prima facie satisfaction that the suit is maintainable or not barred by law, subject to exceptional circumstances requiring temporary protection to prevent irreparable harm or frustration of proceedings.
